descriptions.apps.app-garden: An operator browses the App Garden's curated application templates, deploys apps into the environment, monitors the resulting instances, and retires deployments — turning application delivery into a platform operation with a click-to-deploy experience instead of manual container commands. Deployed apps get stable HTTPS URLs through the platform gateway and, where they use AI, are wired to deployed models automatically.
descriptions.apps.deployment-baseline: What a deployment shipped with is a packaged, digest-identified record, not an inference from whatever the catalog holds now. This validates that record before trusting it and retains its members as the deployment's baseline.
descriptions.apps.release-digest-pinning: An operator who needs every app image addressed by digest rather than by tag can turn that requirement on. A newly published release that does not meet it is refused at publish time.
descriptions.apps.sandbox-workload-provider: An extension that runs code can be placed on either the standard Kubernetes workload backend or on an Agent Sandbox warm pool, chosen per extension.
descriptions.auth.enterprise-sso: Users authenticate through the customer's identity provider — OIDC providers brokered via the platform Keycloak, SAML federations with metadata, SP-initiated login, ACS, and single logout, and edge-terminated client-certificate (CAC/PKI smartcard) login — with platform-managed sessions, token refresh, and logout, so access is enterprise identity end to end. The analyst-side login steps and the admin-side wiring steps converge on the same mechanism from both ends.
descriptions.auth.local-user-administration: An administrator manages the platform's local accounts directly: creating a user who can sign in, reading and listing accounts, changing an account's details, resetting its password, and removing it. Non-administrators are refused listing accounts, reading their own account, trying to grant themselves the admin role, and resetting or removing their own account; refusals against other accounts, and of other updates, were not measured. This is the account lifecycle an operator runs for users who do not come from an external identity provider.
descriptions.auth.personal-access-tokens: Scripts, CI pipelines, and long-lived integrations cannot hold an interactive session. Personal access tokens are the supported alternative: a user mints a token, uses it to authenticate SDK and API clients, and revokes it by id when it is no longer needed.
descriptions.auth.session-revocation: A signed-in user logs out to end their own session. An administrator removes the platform's tracked session records, either one session by id or every session a subject holds. The two actions are not equivalent. A logout that carries the refresh token made that refresh token unusable (measured on earlier builds). Removing a tracked record does not, by itself, invalidate tokens that were already issued (see Conditions and limits).
descriptions.authz.rebac-access-control: Access to platform resources is decided by relationship tuples, subject and group administration, and attribute gates: administrators manage tuples and subjects, applications ask check-access questions and receive decisions with recorded reasons, datasets carry attribute-gate bindings evaluated per caller, and every decision is logged — the policy layer the security docs ship as ReBAC, deny-by-default over an explicit subject → relation → object model.
descriptions.catalog.dataset-registry: Datasets and their containers are first-class catalog entities with URNs, schemas, and search — operators register onboarded sources so applications and analysts find governed data by name rather than by connection string. The catalog is the description layer, deliberately apart from connector configuration (transport) and from secrets management; it is also the namespace other capabilities address: retrieval jobs target dataset URNs, and attribute gates bind to them.
descriptions.catalog.registered-sources: Register S3 and PostgreSQL sources, then scan into the governed catalog.
descriptions.catalog.secrets-management: Service-account keys that live in application configuration are the credentials that leak. Kamiwaza stores the credentials used by connectors, tools, and services as catalog secrets instead — URN-addressed, created and retrieved through a governed API, and stored encrypted rather than held in plaintext config.
descriptions.catalog.writable-datasets: Manage file content inside platform-managed datasets.
descriptions.connectors.ai-assisted-connector-setup: Use a selected model to propose or attempt connector setup and bounded repair, with live preview and revision checks.
descriptions.connectors.connector-builder: Import OpenAPI, Postman, documentation or PDF text into a connector project; test its definition, generate a tool package and deploy a dedicated connector runtime.
descriptions.connectors.managed-data-sources: An operator onboards data sources as managed connectors: browsing a typed catalog of connector manifests, creating connector configurations from it, registering new connector types and already-running connector instances, and maintaining the fleet — so analysts discover and use sources through a governed surface instead of raw credentials. Configuration is exposed in the admin UI (Settings, Data Connectors), on the platform API under /connectors, and through the SDK's typed ConnectorsService.
descriptions.connectors.oauth-tool-policies: An app owner or administrator sets, for one app installation, tool and provider, the list of provider operations the tool may call through the OAuth broker, such as gmail.search without gmail.send. On the broker's standard proxy path, a call whose operation is not on that list is refused.
descriptions.connectors.user-oauth-authorization: An analyst authorizes a connector against their own identity: the platform drives the provider's OAuth flow — redirect or device code, per the connector's manifest — completes it on a public callback, and stores the resulting tokens server-side, so per-user sources like Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace are accessed as the user, under the user's own entitlements, rather than as a shared service account. An in-process OAuth broker then mints short-lived, lease-tracked provider tokens for downstream consumers, keeping refresh tokens and client secrets inside the platform.
descriptions.context.dataset-indexing: Bind a catalog dataset to a searchable semantic/lexical index.
descriptions.context.workroom-ingestion-summary: A workroom member who can view the workroom reads one summary of what has been ingested into it: how many data sources it has, broken down by source type, when the earliest and latest sources were created, the total error count across those sources, and how many catalog datasets are tagged to the workroom.
descriptions.context.workroom-raw-file-store: Store, list, read and update workroom raw files.
descriptions.delegation.brokered-resource-access: The moment software is given a credential to reach data, the credential's blast radius becomes the software's blast radius, and every later access is attributable only to the credential. This capability keeps the secret away from the workload: a run reaches datasets and model deployments through brokered, run-scoped endpoints, exercising a credential binding rather than possessing a credential, and each use is recorded.
descriptions.delegation.capability-grants: Ambient authority is the failure mode this capability exists to prevent: software that can do whatever the credential it holds can do, with no record of what it was actually permitted. Here, what a delegated workload may do is issued as an explicit capability contract against a published catalog of capabilities, and the resulting grants can be listed and read back. The permission is a thing you can point at, not an emergent property of a token.
descriptions.delegation.consent-and-approval-gates: The question a governance reviewer asks first about delegated software is whether a person can stand between it and a consequential action. This capability is that interposition point: a workload declares an intent, a human decision is recorded against that intent before the work proceeds, and a higher-risk effect can carry a separate approval. Withdrawing the workload's registration stops the whole arrangement.
descriptions.delegation.pending-approval-queue: An approver lists the delegated-workload effects in their tenant that are waiting for a human decision, polls that list from the SDK, and approves or denies an effect from it. The queue is an API and SDK surface; no approval inbox ships in the UI.
descriptions.delegation.run-claims-lifecycle: Delegated work that leaves no trail cannot be audited, and a trail reconstructed from logs after the fact is not the same as a record the execution path was required to produce. Here a run is reserved, claimed by the workload that will execute it, and moved through explicit transitions until it completes or is cancelled. The effects a run intends to have are reserved before they happen, so the record is a product of execution rather than a reconstruction of it.
descriptions.delegation.workload-identity-and-attesta: When software acts on a user's behalf, the usual shortcut is to hand it the user's credential — after which nothing downstream can tell the two apart. This capability removes that shortcut. A delegated workload is attested against its own Kubernetes deployment identity, receives capability material bound to a proof-of-possession key it holds, and is verified by resource servers against a published key set. The workload's actions are attributable to the workload, and a stolen assertion is not replayable by a holder that cannot prove possession of the key.
descriptions.extensions.developer-path: The question behind this capability is whether a customer's own developers can extend the platform, or whether every new capability is a request to the vendor. A developer scaffolds an extension with kz-ext, iterates against a live cluster, and publishes it so the platform lists and runs it as a first-class resource.
descriptions.federation.cluster-pairing: Multi-site deployments need clusters that interoperate without either side surrendering control of its own data. Pairing establishes that relationship explicitly: two clusters are joined into a federation, the receiving cluster chooses how it will verify callers from the other side, and an allowlist governs which subjects it will broker at all. The relationship is inspectable and reversible.
descriptions.federation.execution-gates: The question a receiving cluster has to answer about federated work is whether it consents to spending its own compute on a caller from somewhere else. Execution gates are where that decision lives. The federated job service consults a pluggable gate before dispatching any job, and the policy sits with the cluster that owns the resources rather than with the cluster making the request.
descriptions.federation.federated-retrieval: The sovereignty question in a multi-site deployment is whether analysis requires moving data. Here it does not: an analyst discovers datasets on a paired cluster and runs retrieval there, the remote cluster's own catalog and retrieval services process the request against its own adapters, and only the results come back. The data stays where its owner keeps it.
descriptions.federation.remote-jobs: Work runs where the data lives: jobs are submitted to a paired cluster synchronously or asynchronously, monitored, cancelled, and their results and logs retrieved, with mesh-proxied transport carrying the calls between clusters and the receiving cluster keeping authorization in its own hands. Execution is authorized before compute is spent, and gated results are filtered per caller before release.
descriptions.ingestion.document-translation: Translate parsed Markdown into a requested language through a configured model and retrieve persisted language artifacts.
descriptions.ingestion.multimedia-extraction: Media-heavy files are parsed on the way in: the context service routes image, audio, and video inputs through the OmniParse extension for OCR-and-vision-oriented extraction, transcription, and video analysis, so a scanned page, a recording, or a video lands in the same searchable substrate as a text document. An audio-readiness probe tells a workroom — before anyone uploads — whether transcription is actually available, with a remediation-carrying answer when it is not.
descriptions.ingestion.parse-from-url: OmniParse downloads a document from a public HTTP or HTTPS URL on the server and stores it as a document record. The caller then reads the record as Markdown or HTML, or reads its chunks, tables or figures, through the same document routes used for uploaded files. Tables, figures and chunks are declared in ingestion.structured-document-outputs.
descriptions.ingestion.scheduled-ingest: Ingestion runs on demand: a registered source type is ingested immediately through one call, a DDE connector's ingest is triggered per connector, and the results land as catalog datasets owned by the requester. A job-registration API with cron syntax and pollable status exists alongside — but read the not_supported entry before claiming schedules: at the pinned revision registered jobs are stored, not executed.
descriptions.ingestion.security-markings: When an operator configures a marking provider, the data engine parses the marking on each ingested document through that provider, evaluates it against the source's level boundary, and attaches the validated marking to the record rather than dropping it at the door. Core itself carries no marking grammar: without a provider (the default), provider-managed marked input is refused. The deprecated security_marking-only input remains accepted as uninterpreted legacy metadata.
descriptions.ingestion.structured-document-outputs: Expose structured tables, figure metadata and text chunks from supported parsed documents.
descriptions.ingestion.video-frame-analysis: Upload a video to OmniParse as an asynchronous job. The job pulls keyframes and the audio track out of the video, asks a vision model to describe each keyframe, transcribes the audio, and stores the keyframe images, descriptions and transcript for retrieval.
descriptions.kaizen.admin-settings-console: Inspect effective configuration and change/reset audited settings.
descriptions.kaizen.agent-auto-routing: Kaizen can bring one specialist agent into a chat turn to help the agent serving it, picked on the server from the agents that serving agent may call. Each member can pin the agent that serves their chats, allow specialist help for it, and leave agents out of that pinned agent's specialist help. Specialist help is a consult: the serving agent keeps the turn and the answer.
descriptions.kaizen.agent-packages: An administrator pins a package at a vetted version, the platform stores a frozen copy, and agents are granted capability from those packages rather than from whatever a registry serves today.
descriptions.kaizen.agent-publication-approval: Members submit agent and package proposals; a Kaizen administrator approves or rejects them, and can later disable, re-enable or roll back an agent.
descriptions.kaizen.answer-feedback: Members give a thumbs up or thumbs down on a chat answer. Kaizen records the vote as an audit event that administrator metrics count.
descriptions.kaizen.artifacts: Create and revise agent outputs; inspect versions, fork and share permitted artifacts.
descriptions.kaizen.context-compression: Members can opt in to compressing code-execution output, a terse Plain-speak answer style and prompt trim, see estimated savings, and compact a long conversation.
descriptions.kaizen.conversation-event-streaming: An integration opens a Kaizen conversation's live event stream (server-sent events) instead of polling, replays events after a journal position, and can send a message and wait for the agent's reply over that stream. This is the primary Kaizen 0.7.1 conversation contract, reached through the platform SDK.
descriptions.kaizen.conversation-search: Search authorized conversations and navigate document/project results in primary Kaizen.
descriptions.kaizen.custom-agents: Specialised assistants should be something an analyst builds, not something they file a ticket for. In Kaizen Legacy an analyst creates a named agent, gives it instructions, chooses its model, and binds skills to it from the skills library — configuration rather than an engineering request.
descriptions.kaizen.data-chat: An analyst asks questions in a Kaizen Legacy conversation and gets synthesized answers grounded in workroom data — uploaded files, admin-configured Microsoft 365 sources, and MCP tools — with follow-up turns, resumable conversations, and conversation lifecycle managed through the platform SDK. This is the daily-driver analytic question-and-answer experience, built over the search substrate claimed separately as context.workroom-document-search.
descriptions.kaizen.document-canvas-export: A member opens one of their own uploaded documents in an editable canvas, and can export the current text as Markdown, Word (DOCX) or PDF through the API; the web app has no export control at this revision. Edits made in the canvas are saved as new versions through the artifact revision route, which kaizen.artifacts declares.
descriptions.kaizen.document-collections: Maintain named document collections for primary Kaizen library and grounding workflows.
descriptions.kaizen.member-token-budget: When an operator sets a positive daily cap, Kaizen refuses a member's direct model calls for the rest of the UTC day once that member's recorded token use reaches it. No cap is set by default.
descriptions.kaizen.metrics-dashboard: Read primary Kaizen administrator metrics, usage snapshots and separately audited member-usage summaries.
descriptions.kaizen.multi-agent-orchestration: Coordinate specialist child work with bounded plans and durable traces.
descriptions.kaizen.notifications-inbox: List member notifications and mark one/all read.
descriptions.kaizen.platform-operator-tools: Closed SDK tools inspect platform resources and preview/apply bounded Demo Blueprint actions.
descriptions.kaizen.prebuilt-agents: Kaizen ships four ready-made agents (Web Researcher, Software Engineer, Ontology Builder and Demo Builder), provisions them at startup, and publishes them to every member.
descriptions.kaizen.privacy-guard: Kaizen Legacy's Privacy Guard checks a chat message in the browser before it is sent. In warn mode it shows the user the likely emails, phone numbers, Social Security numbers, IPv4 addresses and secrets it found and lets them choose what to send. In redact mode it replaces each one with <REDACTED> and sends the result.
descriptions.kaizen.product-identity: Kaizen v3 and Kaizen v4 are separate products that share catalog names. This decides which product a given release is, and whether a claimant on a reserved Kaizen name is the genuine article.
descriptions.kaizen.projects: Group conversations and library pointers in member-authorized projects.
descriptions.kaizen.prompt-library-and-chains: Save member prompts and validate/run versioned chains.
descriptions.kaizen.recipes: In Kaizen Legacy a user can save a tool call from search results as a named recipe that keeps the call's arguments and result. Every agent gets a recipe lookup tool that searches the saved recipes by tool name or keyword, so it can repeat a call that worked before.
descriptions.kaizen.scheduled-tasks: Preview/create owner-bound task definitions and schedule or background agent work.
descriptions.kaizen.shared-chat-typing-indicators: In a Kaizen chat shared with other members, each participant sees which other members are present and which of them are typing.
descriptions.kaizen.workroom-notes: In Kaizen Legacy, analysts can create Markdown notes in a workroom and edit notes and other text files in a side-pane editor, and the chat agent can create notes with its create_note tool. Notes are files named kaizen-notes/<slug>.md in the workroom's file list.
descriptions.models.discover-and-download: An operator searches model hubs from Kamiwaza, inspects a model's files and quantization variants, and downloads the selected artifacts into the platform with trackable per-file status. This is the acquisition on-ramp for every local deployment: what it establishes is that open-weight models can be pulled into the platform deliberately — with file selection, progress visibility, and access control — not whether they can then be served (that is models.local-deployment).
descriptions.models.external-endpoints: An operator fronts existing inference-provider contracts with Kamiwaza: for OpenAI-compatible and Azure hosts a discovery wizard validates the endpoint URL and credentials, enumerates the models the provider exposes, and registers the selected ones; for AWS Bedrock and AWS Transcribe a setup form registers the model the operator names — after which they deploy through the normal model lifecycle and serve through the same OpenAI-compatible routes, audit, and access-control surfaces as locally hosted models. This is Path B beside local hosting (Path A): "can we front our existing provider contracts with Kamiwaza?" is claimable and deniable independently of "can we host models ourselves?".
descriptions.models.gpu-placement: When a model is deployed on an install that has the placement operator enabled, Kamiwaza decides where it runs — which node, which GPU or memory pool, and how much memory to reserve — so that a cluster's accelerators serve more than one model deliberately rather than by accident. The platform estimates the model's VRAM footprint, classifies the hardware it could land on, reserves a budget there, and refuses fast and legibly when nothing fits. The deploy flow itself is unchanged: on such an install placement is a property of every deploy, not a separate operation.
descriptions.models.local-deployment: An operator takes a downloaded model through its full serving lifecycle on cluster hardware: deploy with an automatically selected (or explicitly chosen) engine, observe the launch through a documented status vocabulary, read logs and typed error codes when something goes wrong, and stop or retire the deployment. A novice mode fronts the same lifecycle with curated defaults. Where the model lands — node, GPU, memory budget — is models.gpu-placement; models the platform does not host are models.external-endpoints.
descriptions.models.openai-compatible-inference: Applications call Kamiwaza-governed models — locally served or externally proxied — through OpenAI-compatible routes, so anything written against the OpenAI wire format runs against them without code changes. The SDK makes this concrete by handing back a standard openai.OpenAI client already pointed at a chosen deployment. This compatibility claim is distinct from deployment: it is the claim application developers actually ask about, and it can hold or fail independently of whether deploys succeed.
descriptions.models.tenant-mode-inference: Tenant mode (the 1.3.0 "Tenant Mode Inference" work) lets a cluster owner give a namespaced Kamiwaza tenant local model serving without granting it permission to read Nodes and without installing any cluster-scoped GPU component in the tenant release. The owner publishes an Ed25519-signed compute-profile bundle that attests the hardware and binds each profile to an exact Kubernetes resource. Core verifies the bundle before sizing and again at dispatch, derives a CPU or GPU request from the model, and places it on an owner binding: a whole device, a qualified MIG slice, or an accounted VRAM share. When the owner enables the feature, every local deployment takes this path; nothing falls back to the legacy placement path.
descriptions.models.tensor-parallel-serving: A model too large for one GPU can be served by vLLM sharded across several GPUs on the same node. The operator sets tensor_parallel_size in the model configuration and vLLM starts with --tensor-parallel-size N; how many GPUs the deployment reserves for it depends on the launch path (for the legacy and Docker paths, see Supported operations and Conditions and limits). On Kubernetes, core's count check and the placement planner can refuse a request that does not fit rather than start it with the wrong shard count; which check applies, and whether any does, depends on the path and on the GPU count core detects (see Conditions and limits). The answer to "can you serve a 70B model across four GPUs?" is this capability; the answer to "can one vLLM replica span two machines?" is models.two-node-serving, a different mechanism.
descriptions.models.two-node-serving: An administrator attaches a second GPU node to the head node over SSH. The serving engines can then start model containers on that node, copy downloaded model files to it, and report its GPUs in the cluster capabilities. The source describes the setup as meant for DGX Spark and similar machines.
descriptions.platform.access-requests: Request resource access and record grantor approval/denial.
descriptions.platform.admin-copilot: A platform copilot answers a system administrator's operational questions through an authenticated thread-and-run API. What makes it claimable is not the model behind it but the contract around it: durable run states, explicit confirmation before any write, capability-filtered actions, budgets, and audit records tagged with a copilot policy.
descriptions.platform.airgapped-install: Classified and sovereign environments cannot reach the internet, and an installer that assumes a public registry is an installer they cannot use. At the cited revisions Kamiwaza's disconnected path is an ordinary Helm install that pulls from the customer's own registry: the release chart and the images it lists are copied into that registry by digest, and a small set of values points every image, and the App Garden catalog, inside the network.
descriptions.platform.api-reference: Serve machine-readable OpenAPI and offline interactive reference.
descriptions.platform.app-generation-path: A developer builds an application against the Kamiwaza platform through a single tool-supported path: scaffold a working application with kz-ext create, iterate on it locally with kz-ext dev local, check it with kz-ext validate, and deploy it to a connected instance with kz-ext dev. The application the path produces is not a blank project — it is built against the SDK runtime contract from the first commit: platform-injected identity, workroom scoping, and typed boundary errors are wired into the generated code, so what the developer customizes is already a correctly-integrated Kamiwaza application.
descriptions.platform.greymatter-mesh-integration: Where a customer already runs GreyMatter Core, Kamiwaza can use GreyMatter instead of Istio as its service mesh and ingress routing provider. Routes for deployed models, apps, tools and extensions are published by a GitOps route writer: core renders deterministic generated configuration and commits it to the tenant branch that GreyMatter's configuration manager reconciles, so no platform-admin step is needed per route. Edge requests on protected routes are authenticated by a GreyMatter external-authorization call back into Kamiwaza. Whether a given route is protected depends on who wrote it and when: see "Protected and bypass routes" under Conditions and limits. GreyMatter Core itself is the customer's; Kamiwaza does not install it.
descriptions.platform.kubernetes-install: Before any capability matters, a customer has to be able to stand the platform up on hardware they own. This is that claim at the level a customer actually asks it — can we install this on our infrastructure, and does it run across more than one machine — with the system requirements stated as conditions rather than aspirations.
descriptions.platform.licensing-and-eula: Validate signed license files and surface commercial-term status.
descriptions.platform.news-feed: Display configured vendor news with offline fallback.
descriptions.platform.observability: An operator responding to a problem needs to see what the platform is doing without shelling into nodes, and an enterprise needs that telemetry in the tooling it already runs. Both are addressed: logs are readable through the UI and per-deployment APIs, a single endpoint summarizes which platform resources are configured, and OpenTelemetry ships traces and metrics outward.
descriptions.platform.operations-and-notifications: Read persistent per-user operations and notification feeds.
descriptions.platform.tenant-namespace-install: A customer platform team that grants only a pre-created namespace, not cluster-admin, can install Kamiwaza there with one Helm release run by a namespace-admin identity. In this tenant-direct mode the release creates only namespaced objects and holds no permission to read Nodes; the platform team provides the namespace, security-context bindings, storage class, pull credentials, supplemental installer Roles, the mesh or edge and, where the GreyMatter sidecar path requires them, the Kubernetes API egress CIDRs beforehand. Red Hat OpenShift (ROSA, ARO) is the reference target: there the tenant base overlay sets restrictedV2AssignedUid so pods can take platform-assigned UIDs under restricted-v2, the chart's shared pod security-context helper and Kamiwaza's extension pods drop their fixed UIDs, and the egress policies the extension runtime writes for extension pods allow OpenShift DNS (the core chart's own egress policies, opt-in and off in this lane, have no port-53 rule except one to kube-system). Core's own model-serving pods -- the legacy adapters' (vLLM, llama.cpp, whisper.cpp, diffusion) and the tenant-mode workloads' alike -- still set runAsUser: 65532 and a fixed fsGroup (the literal is present in the legacy Kubernetes adapters at the cited core revision; the tenant-mode workloads were not re-read), so admitting them depends on the security-context bindings the platform team provides. A disconnected install can use a tenant OCI bundle imported into the OpenShift registry.
descriptions.platform.usage-and-audit: Answering "who did what, and when" during an audit depends on the events having been recorded before anyone asked. The platform records user activity and authorization decisions, and exposes a recent-activity feed over API and SDK — the raw material an audit response is built from.
descriptions.retrieval.async-retrieval-jobs: Retrieval against registered datasets runs as asynchronous jobs: create a job against a dataset URN, poll or cancel it, stream results over SSE, or pull columnar batches over Arrow Flight — so a large retrieval is an operation with a lifecycle, ownership, and access checks, not a blocking query. Source coverage at the pinned revision spans filesystem, S3, Hive, Postgres, Kafka, Slack, and platform-managed datasets, each behind its own adapter.
descriptions.security.consent-and-banners: Administrators configure a pre-login consent gate and persistent classification banners — banner text and colors, consent content, and acceptance flow — and extend the same markings to embedded and extension apps through a single embeddable script. This gives deployments the SYSTEM HIGH labeling and acknowledged-use posture their accreditation requires, with acceptance recorded server-side for audit when the acceptance request reaches the server. The accreditor's question this answers is "does every surface show the approved banner and require the acknowledgment?" — not a question about endpoints.
descriptions.skills.skills-library: Agent skills — packaged agent behaviors (a SKILL.md instruction package an AI agent loads and follows), not workforce competencies or personnel skill records — are imported, listed, curated, exported singly or as bundles, and deleted through a platform skills library, so teams share vetted agent behaviors across workrooms and applications instead of rebuilding them per app. The library is its own claim, deliberately separate from the agents that consume skills: it can exist and be evidenced without Kaizen, and the team-scope sharing demand requires exactly that separation.
descriptions.tools.mcp-tool-shed: An operator deploys MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool servers from container images or curated Tool Shed templates, reads their deployment status, and discovers what is running — so agents and applications call governed, platform-managed tool endpoints instead of ad-hoc ones. Each deployed tool server gets a stable HTTPS URL usable by any MCP-compatible client.
descriptions.workrooms.create: An analyst creates their own workroom — naming it, describing it, and choosing its persistence posture — without operator involvement. Creation is exposed in the Workroom Manager UI, on the platform API (POST /workrooms/), and as a first-class SDK call (WorkroomService.create), so both interactive users and automation can provision workrooms.
descriptions.workrooms.org-decommission: An administrator lists the organization's workrooms, creates a decommission plan with a future cutoff, and confirms it by typing the organization name. Creating the plan turns off room creation. Confirmation archives every planned room and makes rooms read-only. At the cutoff the rooms are deleted. A tombstone keeps each room's name, cutoff and retention contact.
